children.name: Long before they were bankers to popes a
children.characters: Long before they were bankers to popes and kings, the Medici traded wool. Their shops in the Mercato Vecchio dealt with suppliers from England to Flanders, and the profits gave them a foothold in the city's powerful guilds.

children.name: Membership of the Arte della Lana brough
children.characters: Membership of the Arte della Lana brought political rights as well as trade. By the 1390s the family sat on the city's governing councils.

children.name: Giovanni di Bicci turned that foothold i
children.characters: Giovanni di Bicci turned that foothold into a bank. By 1400 the family business lent money, changed currencies and moved funds for merchants across Europe.

children.name: Imagine you are advising a Florentine me
children.characters: Imagine you are advising a Florentine merchant in 1430. He wants to sell cloth in London and buy alum in Rome, but he does not want to carry gold across Europe.

children.name: Using what you learned about the Medici
children.characters: Using what you learned about the Medici Bank, explain how he could use the bank's network to complete both deals. What risks would the bank take on, and how did the Medici protect themselves from those risks?

children.name: Bills of exchange let him pay into the M
children.characters: Bills of exchange let him pay into the Medici branch in Florence and collect in London and Rome without moving gold. The bank earned fees and exchange-rate margins but carried credit and currency risk; branches were separate partnerships with local managers, which limited the losses of any one branch.
